Kneading the stub of his cigarette into the worn-out ashtray, Winston's gaze flitted between the photographs in front of him. A bowling alley, deserted, save for a solitary figure slumped over in the congealing slick of his own blood – the scene drenched in a chilling morbidity. 

His suspect was Mia, a waitress at the bowling alley. The late shift was her domain; her eyes, always heavy-lidded with fatigue, had fallen on a familiar figure, Joel, numbingly often. The man had his peculiar habits, including late-night bowling. Mia had a keen knowledge of that; it wasn’t easy to overlook when they regularly crossed paths during her shifts, Joel’s ball thundering and skidding down the shiny lanes.

Fiddling with a small, old key on his desk, Winston’s thought went back to his first meeting with Mia. He had found the key while cleaning her table after an interview and asked her about it. Almost flippantly, she mentioned it was for a private mausoleum in the nearby cemetery. The location was within walking distance from her workplace, an old cemetery cloaked in a gloom that seemed centuries old. The eerie part was her odd ritual; post her shift, her coworkers attested to seeing her trudge towards the graveyard regularly, a private pilgrimage in the dead of night.

Winston vividly remembered his surprise when he had found nunchaku, a pair of them, while searching Mia's home. The night visits to the cemetery coupled with the ominous presence of the martial arts weapon was undoubtedly unsettling. Unraveling further, he found out Mia had been practicing and honing her skills with the nunchaku at home, late into the night. For years, she had been devoted to martial arts, with a particular emphasis on the nunchaku, the significance of which crept up on him like a poisonous vine. Her gym was known for teaching the use of this weapon.

"I suspect you're quite adept at swinging these," Winston had said to Mia, gesturing towards the nunchaku that lay on the table between them when he'd confronted her about it later. 

Mia had smiled enigmatically, her eyes twinkling with the lethality of secrets untold. "Keep your eyes open, detective," she had replied, her voice a chilling sotto voce lingering between them, hang enough in the suffocating silence.

His thoughts whirling, Winston stubbed out the last of his cigarette. The available evidence was yet⟦ to⟧ form a coherent story, but Mia was conspicuous. He had ventured into labyrinthian investigations before, but the mystery of Joel's murder felt like uncharted territory. Winston felt a shiver creep into his spine as he got ready for round two with Mia.

Winston stepped into the dimly lit bowling alley, prowling between lanes like a panther on the hunt. An unusual place to be hammered to death, he thought, especially during the graveyard shift, but a good detective never questioned the chosen venues or the hour of the city's grim reaper. Winston surveyed the empty building, the only sound being that of his own boots echoing off the polished hardwood.

The bartender, one Rosemary – if her nameplate could be trusted – was scrubbing down a countertop at the far corner of the bar. Winston walked over, took a seat on one of the bar stools and introduced himself. 

"I hear you were working here the night Joel was killed," he mentioned, as he watched her movements. 

Rosemary looked up, her face impassive, "Yes, that's true. It was my usual midnight shift, and Joel got murdered after we had closed down for the night. Wasn't much else to do."

"You seem to have keys to this place," Winston noticed, spotting a set of keys on the counter. 

"Yes, I do, for closing hours," she replied, sliding the keys back into her jeans pocket.

He continued his questions, "I understand you practice martial arts, Rosemary?"

For the first time, Rosemary stopped her cleaning and smiled, "Yes, that's right. In fact, I work out regularly at a martial arts gym. Nunchaku workshops are my favorite," she added, her eyes twinkling with something akin to pride.

Winston nodded, imparting no judgement on her preferred pastime. 

Suddenly, a glint at the corner of the room caught his attention. A collection of weaponry displayed on a wall. Upon closer look, he recognized various martial arts weapons, including a pair of nunchaku.

“My father was a big fan of martial arts. He left me his collection," explained Rosemary, noticing his interest. "In fact, the nunchaku you see hanging on the wall is part of my personal collection."

As Winston stood up to leave, he turned to Rosemary, "Did you know Joel well?"

She hesitated for a moment, her eyes downcast, "Joel... he was a good friend. He always wanted to help. And he was the one person who could save me from this terrible debt I'm wrestling with. But to my despair, he... he said no when I asked him for a loan."

Winston pulled his sedan into the dusty lot of the low-rise motel on the outskirts of town. There he saw Tessa, emerging from a room and handing a key back to the motel manager. The motel staff confirmed that the implicating room was indeed paid for by Tessa, and their logbook showed that she had checked in before Frederick’s death. They also agreed that she had remained on the premises throughout.

The day Tessa was arrested, she displayed her usual calm demeanor. As the police handcuffed her, a metallic shine of a corkscrew slipped out from her apron pocket, landing on the ground below. This was her personal corkscrew, a tool she always had on hand for her routine work at the restaurant, and one that she was seen using frequently to open wine bottles during her shift.

As Winston left the motel to return to the precinct, he mused over the victim’s connection with Tessa. Frederick knew about Tessa’s considerable debt, and this was not ordinary behavior between a server and a regular patron. But for now, the facts just laid out the circumstances. His sole contribution to this puzzle would be to compile the facts so they could make sense. The rest — the swift execution of justice — was a matter of time. And Winston knew that time always brought the truth to light.

Winston straightened his tie as he approached the scene of Frederick's murder, squinting under the motel's harsh fluorescent lighting. Frederick, a successful events planner, was stealing lucrative contracts right from Van’s territory. On the other hand, Van also managed to poach a few of Frederick's prime clients. Frederick's competitors saw his success as the rising spark of a problem they had to deal with. Someone like Van, maybe. 

Van. The one who was always behind a desk at every event he planned, for some reason avoiding any kind of physical exertion. For instance, at every event, he could be found refusing a spot in the robust, physically-demanding relay races that colleagues customarily participated in. That night was no different, the event was a wine tasting. Van would likely be there, not participating in the traditional grape-stomping competition. There, Van would flaunt his newly-acquired clients; the ones he had usurped from Frederick.

With this thought in his head, Winston drove over to the event, arriving to the sight of Van pouring wine expediently with a corkscrew for the event attendees instead of joining in on the active games. 

"Van," Winston greeted, nodding at him.

"Detective," Van replied, raising an eyebrow. 

He paused as Winston took a seat in front of him, then offered a bottle of red. "Wine, Detective?"

"No, thanks," Winston said, "Don't you usually have an assistant to open wine bottles?"

Van laughed, shrugging off the observation easily. "I like doing it. It's therapeutic," he said.

Then there was the fresh dressing peeking out from under Van's cuff, the one he offered some vague explanation for, just like every other time Winston had seen him injured. He referred to these as ‘small accidents’.

He remembered what Van's colleagues had said about him. Always getting injured, never playing in any games, always behind a desk, and there was that thing with Frederick. 

"Frederick," Winston started, both men looking somber at the mention of the recent murder. Van averted his gaze, focusing steadfastly on the bottle he was opening.

"I heard you had a falling out."

Van sighed,⟦ and⟧ for the first time that evening he looked tired. "Fred and I... we had our differences. He was snatching clients right under my nose. And I wasn't just taking it lying down, I got back at him by snatching some of his clients,” he confessed. 

"Heard you even threatened him once," Winston said quietly.

"That was just business, nothing personal," Van replied coldly. "If you're suggesting--"

Winston lifted his hands, chuckling lightly. "I'm not suggesting anything, Van," he said carefully.

Turning his attention back to the bottle, Van popped the cork and poured himself a glass. "Fine. I had my disagreements with Frederick," he admitted. "Yes, we threatened each other over clients. But that's all it was... just threats."

In the quiet isolation of a remote chalet, Cecilia's life brutally ended by an axe and it's now up to the jaded Detective Winston to untangle a web of deceit involving suspects, Stuart and Alice.

Winston wrinkled his now weather-beaten brow, his dark eyes hard and focused as he stood at the outskirts of the secluded chalet. The sight of Cecilia's body, found long after the time Stuart was noted alone at the site lent a sense of unease that still imprinted in his mind from the crime scene photos.

There was a strange quiet that persisted in the area as the evening shadows coalesced further into night. Winston was particularly interested in the electrical works of the chalet, the severed power cables indicative of Stuart’s well-known method of using his axe to cut them. All conveniently hidden behind walls and ceilings but paramount in their purpose. He was reminded that important clues sometimes lurk in the most innocuous of places.

Winston glanced around, his gaze settling on Stuart lumbering towards him. As usual, the man had his tool bag over one sturdy shoulder, the familiar shape of an axe imprinted onto its side. Its weight was seemingly imprinted onto Stuart’s posture, yet worn with a sense of profound solidarity. A sense of familiarity, born from years of dedication to his profession and the meticulous demand for his specialized tools, such as axes.

“Stuart?” Winston enquired, attempting to mirror a casual air.

“Yeah, that would be me,” Stuart responded, his respect for the detective's powerful presence evident.

“You've been working on this property?”

“Sure have,” the large man nodded, setting his tool bag into the dirt nearby. The soft clink of tools echoed faintly in the silent expanse. Stuart was a proficient electrician, everyone in the county knew. He had harbored resentment against Cecilia, for reasons unknown; a motive that lingered with a subtle hint in the air. His rigor and loyalty to his profession manifested in every job site he touched—an axe always included in his equipment.

A long moment passed, the evening wind whistling in the background. 

"Cecilia, the owner... she⟦ hired⟧ you, didn't she?" Winston broke the silence, his gaze firm on Stuart.

“Yeah... had a bad power outage that day."

"How long did it last?"

"Unusual one. Lasted all day actually."

The chirping of crickets began to build and a layer of frost was slowly painting itself across the chalet’s exterior. This suggested that there were no other workers or inhabitants during the time of Stuart's work.

Winston found himself hooked onto the echo of Stuart's resounding words, stirring question after question in his mind. He wouldn’t voice them; not yet. 

A cold wind blew past the duo, shifting leaves rustled around the chalet whispering secrets that they had witnessed. A secret Winston had set out to uncover. With that, he bid Stuart a goodnight and left the chalet site, the outline of the crime scene etched into his memory as he sped off into the distance; his wearied sights set on tomorrow's set of questions.

Detective Winston sat in his office, a thick folder splayed open in front of him. Inside were various reports about a school counselor named Alice. Alice was evidently no ordinary school counselor - a slew of allegations and complications surrounded her. 

Winston got up, tucked the folder under his arm and headed to the school where Alice was employed.

As he approached the counselor's office, he could hear the muffled sound of murmuring in the hallway around him. Alice was known for her involvement in outdoor activities for students – particularly annual camping trips. Winston glimpsed several pictures of these camping trips on a notice board outside the office, seeing Alice in several of them, even demonstrating axe-use to the students.

He knocked gently before letting himself into Alice’s office. 

“Ms. Alice, I presume?” He asked, to which she nodded. 

There was an air of tension about her. Perhaps it was because she was carrying the burden of an extramarital affair that threatened her standing in the local community and her professional career. It was common knowledge in the school corridors that Alice was on the brink of losing her job due to the scandal. 

The conversation turned to Alice's personal life, Winston asked, "Ms. Alice, it seems you have a fair amount of free time in the evenings?" Alice agreed, mentioning that she spent her evenings alone in a particular room at her house. Her neighbors had reportedly seen her carrying stacks of newspapers into her house, which she hardly ever let anyone in. They claimed to have heard her reading out loud from these newspapers, specifically obituaries, although Winston kept this bit to himself.

The mention of the school's woodshop arose during the conversation, with the principal having reported seeing Alice take an axe from there post-school hours. Alice explained it was a tool demonstration for the camping trips, but Winston noted down the fact, considering the murderer’s weapon – an axe. 

Mention of Cecilia came up, the young girl who had lost her life in a chalet not long ago. Alice didn't seem surprised at the mention of Cecilia, nodding and mentioning about her being one of her students. 

A little bird had earlier mentioned that Cecilia had tripped over Alice’s secret of a grade-changing scandal and had evidence of her infamous extramarital affair. 

As Winston left Alice’s office, he knew the web was much more tangled than what met the eye.<turn|>

Inside the buzzing hubbub of the city's most popular recording studio, Ivan's death by snake venom sends shockwaves through the music realm, forcing the indomitable Detective Winston to pierce the veil of sound and silence, suspects, Timothy and Ricky, echoing in his ears.

The flashing lights and the police tape painted a macabre picture outside the recording studio where Ivan was pronounced dead. Detective Winston stared at the dispatch report and heaved a weary sigh. Highlighted information spelled out a sad tale of love, jealousy, and secrets; especially the ones contained in Timothy's silent confession of an argument where Ivan confronted him about the affair with his girlfriend.

As he entered the studio, a peculiar detail stood out – it was empty when the victim was found. The police had taken the usual preliminary measures, clearing the premises as they went. That detail played a repetitive note in Winston's mind. There was only one name that matched the time of death, Timothy.

Begrudgingly, he agreed to interview Timothy, the victim’s friend and⟦ also⟧ a surfing instructor by trade. Timothy's van was a shrine to waxed boards of all sizes, shapes, and colors, almost like weapons of battle against the waves. When Winston had asked him about it, Timothy fondly explained that every board had its unique purpose, for each wave and beach condition. His job demanded him to know places, waves, and beaches in intimate detail. One could even notice the envy tinged bitterness in Timothy's voice when he shared his love for discovering new surfing spots and how Ivan’s musical success overshadowed his own aspirations.

“What brings you here, detective?” Timothy's voice cut through Winston's thoughts. “Well, you were last seen here with Ivan. You guys…"

“Yeah, we were working on a music project together,” Timothy finished Winston's half-spoken question. His face turned a shade darker as he added, “That was our thing, you know. He did the music, I brought the vibe. But everyone always loved Ivan more, even my own girlfriend.”

There was a certain restlessness in Timothy's manner. His eyes kept darting towards the door, his van in sight. It was always packed and ready; 'to chase the waves,' Timothy had shared during the friendly chit-chat. His resentment towards Ivan had resurfaced, amplified by the fact that Ivan's girlfriend was now in love with him.

When Winston mentioned Ivan's girlfriend, Timothy's smile tightened. Yet when he asked about the argument where Ivan had confronted him about the affair, the smile faded away completely. He didn't want to expose sharper edges of their relationship; the complex, fraught friendship woven with threads of rivalry and jealousy. Most of all, there was a looming fear of Ivan revealing their secret affair to the world.

Winston slowly stood up, giving Timothy a knowing look. He thanked him for his time and walked away, leaving an unsettling silence behind him as Timothy sat, staring at the spot where Ivan used to create music. His secret was a festering wound he had no idea how to treat, and the fear of exposure was a haunting melody he couldn't escape.

At the end of a long day, Winston found himself standing on the bridge, gazing at the dark and unyielding ocean. The carefully collected facts played on repeat, like a song stuck in a loop. He couldn't help but think of Timothy, his passions, his secrets, his fear, his jealousy, and his time at the studio which eerily aligned with the irrevocable end of Ivan's life. A hazy picture began to take form in his mind, but he knew it was far from complete...There were still missing notes in this haunting symphony of death.

Detective Winston stepped out of his car and straightened his tie as he made his way towards the pet shop. An older man stood at the entrance, a look of potential fear and regret on his face. 

"Ricky?" Winston asked with a raised eyebrow.

"Depends who's asking," Ricky responded, eyeing Winston over. 

"Detective Winston," he introduced himself and showed his badge. He noticed a change in Ricky's demeanor. "Might we have a word regarding your business?"

Ricky, swallowing hard, nodded and gestured to the back room of the pet shop. It was filled with a variety of animals, among them a large, intimidating venomous snake settled in a glass tank, aptly showcased as the shop's specialty.

"You seem to have quite a variety of pets here, and appropriate paperwork on display. You do legally own this place, don't you?" Winston asked, pointing at the legal documents hanging on the wall.

Ricky, still unsettled, nodded, "Yes. I also know a bit about venom extraction, which makes this business unique," he added with an attempt at lightheartedness. 

"You know, the police got a tip-off about some illegal activity regarding this pet shop," Winston continued. Ricky's eyes widened.

"Why, I've no idea what you're insinuating detective," Ricky stuttered, looking like a man who feared impending financial and legal repercussions.

"Your financial situation hasn't been the best we've heard," Winston said, "and someone named Ivan has been feeding us some rather interesting information regarding your debts."

"Ivan." Ricky whispered under his breath.

"It seems you had a private meeting with Ivan in an empty recording studio," Winston revealed, seeing Ricky's surprise at this information. "That's where he recorded your conversation, and you confessed to some illegal activities, didn't you?"

Ricky looked down and then glanced up, resignation in his eyes. He nodded somberly, "Yes, Ivan was the only one who knew about the illegal activities... He recorded me talking about the illegal sales and has been blackmailing me with the recording."

Winston thanked Ricky for his time and walked out of the pet shop with much to ponder about this case. One thing was certain - the recording studio where Ricky made his confession was going to be his next stop.<turn|>

In the midst of bustling shoppers, Troy meets his untimely demise by a bear trap, thrusting Detective Winston into a perplexing mall investigation with Alex and Clyde as prime subjects.

Winston stared at the case file on his desk, a half-drunk cup of cold coffee to his side. The victim, Troy, had been found dead in a shopping mall in one of the most unusual circumstances he'd seen: in a bear trap. It was a gruesome scene and one that didn't make much sense.

Confused, Winston made his way to Clyde's auto repair shop. A greasy, dust-covered sign welcoming customers and a few older model cars dotted the yard. The mound of mechanical traps of all kinds added an eerie touch to the scene.

"Clyde," he asked, when a haggard man emerged wiping motor oil off of his hands.

"That's me." came the terse reply.

Winston introduced himself and saw Clyde pause for a moment before shaking his hand. He told him that he wanted to know more about Troy, who according to the information he gathered, was a regular customer at Clyde's.

After a sigh, he nodded, his gaze darkening. "Yeah, Troy was a good customer. Always had car troubles. But he was into me pretty deep... owed me some dough for the work I had done."

Winston then shared a piece of information that Clyde didn't seem privy to - Troy had been at the mall earlier in the day, just before his untimely death.

It was at this point Winston noticed a bear trap amongst the litter of mechanical devices. "You work on those too?" He gestured towards the trap, appearing casual.

Clyde glanced at the trap and nodded. "Sometimes. For pest control and such. People bring them in, they're not workin' right, I fix 'em."

Clyde then went on about how he was on the brink of closing the shop due to his financial struggles. He needed to constantly upgrade his equipment but lacked the necessary funds to do so.

In fact, he too had been at the mall on the same day as Troy. "I was there to buy new equipment for the shop," Clyde added.

It was interesting, Winston thought, given that Clyde's shop was practically a stone's throw away from the location of the murder. He made a mental note to follow-up on that.

As Winston thanked Clyde and turned to leave, he noticed a large sign hanging on the wall with the bold letters stating, "We fix all traps – yes, even bear traps."

Well, he thought to himself, that's a lot of loose ends to tie up. As he walked away, he felt the faint stirrings of a puzzle starting to form. He only hoped he could solve it in time.

Winston, a seasoned police investigator, looked at the shop-till-you-drop nightmare known as a shopping mall - specifically the spot where Troy, a local political leader who proposed specific taxes impacting the horse racing industry, met his untimely demise. The weapon of choice still spun his mind, a bear trap... not something you find in an urban environment. 

He had a long list of suspects, and mall security footage placed next on his interview list, a man named Alex, right there. Alex - a local jockey who runs a business seriously affected by recent economic stress and challenged by the policies and taxes Troy proposed. Alex had been struggling financially for several months, paying out more in expenses than he was earning. Winston had seen intriguing footage of⟦ Alex⟧ grooming Troy's hair at the gathering that night - an odd sight indeed. 

Winston caught the weary Alex, with visible signs of stress, as he was wrapping up his day at the local race track. A taxing industry was even further burdened by the policies Troy supported. They exchanged nods.

"How are you related to Troy?" Winston asked, to initiate their conversation.

"I wasn't really close to him, but we knew each other from the horse race circles. Disagreements happen, everyone has their views," Alex answered ambiguously. 

Looking to probe further into one of his primary leads, Winston continued, "What was your disagreement about exactly?"

"Taxes... policies. Troy proposed this new set of taxes that hit right into my industry," Alex replied, visibly irked, "You’re aware of the dwindling finances of the horse racing, aren't you? I have been paying out more than I have been earning for several months now."

Next, Winston needed to verify some unusual behavior noted by others, "I’ve heard that you have an unusual hobby. Is it true?”

Alex seemed relieved at the change of subject, "Oh yes, quite an unusual hobby; I collect bear traps." 

"Quite an unusual hobby indeed," Winston echoed, playing it cool. 

"After a tedious day at work, I stopped by the mall to shop for some, on the day of the incident," Alex casually mentioned. 

"I see," Winston said, trying not to betray any emotion, already piecing together the facts from the mall security footage, the increased taxes, and the weird yet timely hobby. He made a note and prepared for his next interview.<turn|>

In the dim light of an abandoned factory, Kaylee's lifeless body lay with the cold steel of a pickaxe lodged within, thrusting Detective Winston into a dark game of deception with suspects Penelope and Francis.

Winston breathed a sigh of relief as he entered the comfort of his car, escaping the oppressive heat outside. The day had been anything but a usual one and he reviewed the paper on his clipboard yet again. Kaylee, a young woman, was found dead in an abandoned factory of all places and the purported weapon was a pickaxe, an old miner's pickaxe to be exact.

His next interview was scheduled with a nanny named Penelope. Penelope was not your average nanny. Alongside her formal education in early child care, she also had professional training in the same field, acquiring skills that allowed her to excel in handling children. Despite her credible qualifications, Winston found it decidedly strange to connect a nanny with such a gruesome find, not least because Penelope herself had most of her busy day spent with children, not in an old factory.

After a short walk, he approached a modest suburban home quite close to the abandoned factory. The home itself, despite its proximity, seemed worlds apart from the grim discovery location. 

Penelope greeted him at the door, shaking his hand with a warm smile. "Hello, Penelope." Winston greeted, then a thought hit⟦ him⟧. A person of her profession is typically responsible for a child's growth and upbringing. Penelope's studied and trained background in childcare had indeed stuck in his mind since their last encounter.

During their conversation, Winston learned that Penelope was seen leaving her house around the estimated time of the murder. Interestingly enough, he even had a witness claiming to see Penelope with an old mining pickaxe earlier that day, a claim solidly backed up as the recovered pickaxe, the very same weapon used in the murder, matched exactly the one described by the witness.

Just as he was thinking about the pickaxe, a piece of evidence from the crime scene flashed across his mind. Winston reached into his jacket pocket to pull out a page from a diary. It was from Kaylee's diary. The entry was clear; Kaylee had a meeting scheduled with Penelope at the so-called abandoned factory.

A unease washed over Winston, making the usually delicious coffee taste sour in his mouth. Kaylee seemed to have known something about Penelope that she didn't want public. She had unearthed something about Penelope's past... maybe even criminal past. The parents didn't know... and Kaylee was planning to tell.

He glanced at Penelope, who was sitting across from him, looking anxious. She must've known that the exposure would cause her serious embarrassment... and at worst, cost her her job. With no other events reported that could have prevented Kaylee from meeting Penelope, it all looped back to the meeting at the factory.

"Well, Penelope, I do have a long walk back to my car." he said, finishing the last of his coffee and standing up. "I've taken enough of your time, thank you for your cooperation." He gave a nod as he reached the door, leaving the nanny to contemplate her day filled with children, and his with unanswered questions.

Detective Winston grimaced, finally setting down the carefully documented police case file of the late Kaylee. The coffee stains on the file folder began to bleed into the corners of the cover. The pangs of guilt for indulging in too much work in the form of an overbrewed cup of joe were not his only concern. An image haunted him; it was from a video footage where Francis had caught Kaylee red-handed, threatening his daughter which he digitally recorded as proof.

Shaking the sudden chill from his spine, Winston looked out of his office window to the abandoned factory where Kaylee had been found. Francis, Kaylee's husband, had years of mining experience and was renowned for his pickaxe expertise. Francis had arranged the meeting point and was seen coaxing her into trusting that the factory would be undisturbed.

The town had all been abuzz with this unthinkable murder. Kaylee's constant torment of Francis' daughter, enough to induce anxiety and depression in the child, was now common knowledge. Even more upsetting was the unusual delicateness Francis had shown in handling this situation, a man known for his work involving grueling physical labor that required a high level of strength and endurance.

Digging into his pocket Winston pulled out the receipt for the pickaxe that he'd found in Francis’ pocket, a peculiar coincidence considering Francis’ mining background and the tool associated with it.

In the corner of his foul-smelling, second-hand leather bound desk was a photograph. A crisp, clear frame showing Francis purchasing the said pickaxe at the local hardware store. It was not surprising that Francis had chosen to arm himself with a tool he was already so familiar with, but to invite his wife into a murderous trap of his creation was another level of distressing reality.

Winston looked up to see Francis standing in the doorway, tall and solemn. "Detective Winston," he said quietly, "We need to talk about Kaylee."

Winston nodded, gesturing for him to take a seat. "I heard about what happened. About the threats she made to your daughter."

Francis looked taken aback, his gaze shifting around the room. "Yes...I caught her threatening our daughter. I don't know why she couldn't see what her actions were doing to our daughter."

Winston nodded but said nothing. He stayed silent, letting Francis explain in his own time, about the factory meeting he'd arranged with Kaylee, his knowledge that the factory would have been empty at that time, the purchased pickaxe and the chilling threats Kaylee had aimed towards his daughter.

As Francis left his office, Winston glanced back at the file, picking up the coffee cup, he pondered the gritty mysteries life tended to serve up.<turn|>

When a friendly game of paintball turns fatal with the shocking grenade murder of Ana, seasoned Detective Winston sets out to uncover the hidden truths that lie behind the friendly faces of Troy and Bethany.

Detective Winston counted his steps as he moved between the splattered remains of what was once a thriving paintball field. His thoughts lingered on Ana’s abrupt violence.

Official reports had solidified that aside from the victim, only one other person had been present that tragic night. Troy- the community’s spearheading missionary and the contender in that ill-fated paintball match, was reported to make an unusually early exit, shortly after the deafening explosion that had claimed Ana's life.

Winston knew that Troy had been a missionary in war-torn areas, potentially having rich network of contacts from his time spent abroad. He decided that his next course of action was to pay Troy a visit. He found the man at the local church; brows furrowed and eyes distant, clearly lost in thought. The detective approached slowly, carefully observing the suspect.

Troy looked up, noticing the detective for the first time. “Can I help you, officer?” He asked with an accent Winston could tell came from years spent abroad.

“I believe you can, Troy.” Winston replied, deciding to keep the conversation light. “Must be tough work, serving in war-torn areas.”

Troy shot him a surprised look before relaxing. “It is. But it equips you with skills you never imagined having. Back then, often due to shortage of help, I found myself offering assistance in handling explosives, in case of emergencies.”

Winston made sure to keep his expression neutral; the statement held more weight than Troy probably intended to share. “I understand you were quite involved in the community.”

“Aye, I was. And I hoped to get more involved,” Troy said, a touch of bitterness seeped into his tone, "Ana was unfortunately not supportive of that.”

Detective Winston made a mental note of this as Troy continued, “She was the head, I guess you can say - the ultimate authority in our community. But I feel like, after all my experiences, I could be of more use.”

The church bell chimed, indicating the start of the evening prayer. The detective decided it was a good time to bring up the incident. “You were at the field the day Ana was murdered, weren't you?”

Troy paused for a moment before nodding. "Yes. I was participating in that game. It's heartbreaking what happened to Ana." 

Their conversation wrapped up shortly after with a quiet acknowledgment. Winston knew he was far from solving the case yet, but he knew where to dig deeper. As he left the church, he pondered what lay omitted from Troy’s words.

Perhaps it was due to the prophetic dreams Troy spoke about before Winston left or the rumors he’d heard of Troy being seen browsing black-market weaponry on a clandestine site. Neither fact sat well with the detective.

Winston scanned the kaleidoscope of colored splatters that patterned the paintball field where Ana was last seen alive. The eerie feeling of standing on the same field where his friend lost her life was strange. Ana had been lost here among the harmless shots and splashes of color, in the same tragic game where a crime took place. The same game Bethany had registered for - the same game Bethany played with Ana.

Bethany, Ana’s best friend, was not only well known in this paintball field but also at the military base where she was regularly on duty. Her job there entailed around-the-clock surveillance of the site, ensuring the safe handling of heavy-duty weapons and explosives, including grenades. Bethany's upbringing in the military honed her toughness and her reputation of handling grenades or any other heavy-duty weapons was well taken in the base.

"Mhmm," She said, looking away from him.

"We heard you were good friends with Ana," Winston said, watching as her eyes darted around again. "You were both registered under the same number, you played the same games together. The same game that happened here?"

Her gaze uncomfortably shifted away, "Yes, we were."

Bethany seemed to grow more relaxed as Winston steered the conversation towards light-hearted and non-intrusive topics about paintball games and strategies. Just like others had noticed, her guard would drop a bit, revealing her easy⟦ laughter⟧ and shared anecdotes from past games. But, every time the conversation tips towards personal matters, there was a discernible change in her demeanor, almost a physical reaction, and her eyes darted elsewhere.

"There's something going on that you'd like not to talk about, isn't there Beth?" Winston prodded gently. She quickly shielded herself, and resumed her evasive behavior, eyes avoiding direct contact. Winston looked out at the swamp that had claimed Jess's life. Following the cordoned path, the flash of evidence markers catching his eyes, he ran his fingers around the sai in his hand. It was of a unique make, identical to the style used in Freya's martial arts training and not commonly found. There were not many who could handle such a unique weapon, fewer still who owned them.

The path led him to Freya's home later that day. He was introduced into a crisp and clean living room, save for an empty slot in a display case filled with a fascinating collection of sais. He pondered silently, looking at the missing gap, like a puzzle awaiting to be solved, surely it must have been an important sai to her.

Off the bat, Freya seemed uncomfortable as she started nervously, "It's good to see you detective, I’m sure you've heard from my friends, they stopped by and I expressed to them my concerns about Jess threating to disclose my secrets. They comforted me, assuring me they would speak to her.”

Seeing that Freya seemed distressed, Winston decided to breach the topic divertedly, “Freya, I notice one is missing. Care to tell about it?”

With a hesitant nod, Freya spoke, “It recently went missing. The one missing held a sentimental value to me, Detective.”

"Picked up any replacements?" He asked. “Any practicing recently?”

"Well, I was at my dojo last week for training," Freya offered.

An interesting tidbit given the recent events. He was drawn by a peculiar object on a side table. A phone, separate from the one Freya had nervously returned to her pocket.

“This your personal phone, Freya?” Winston asked.

Freya’s cheeks reddened, and she quickly replied, “That's my private phone, detective. I find it easier to keep my personal lines separated from the world.” The device was quickly turned off, secure under her watchful gaze.

Throughout the conversation, she seemed uncomfortable whenever he moved too close to anything personal, quickly steering to another topic. Noted, Winston thought, but he was yet to bring up anything about Jess.

“Freya, let me cut to the chase. Jess was found to have written a letter to the local paper about exposing someone's dark secrets. We found a large payment from you to a private investigator. Want to tell me something?"

She seemed aghast. "Detective, Jess had been saying for a while that she had something on me that could ruin me. But we all have our secrets, don’t we? I hired someone to figure out what she had, it was all in my defense!”

Winston took a moment to consider her words. She was a charming woman, but he was trained to look past faces. "It's good to be honest, Freya," he added quietly, placing the sai back in the evidence bag and heading for the door. 

Once back in his car, he noted how stalwartly Freya switched off her private phone when he was around, an action that made him ponder as he started his vehicle to return to base.

Winston had never been a huge fan of pop music, he preferred jazz. Nevertheless, he found himself standing next to a stage that had, the previous night, been vibrating with the sound waves of Leona's music. Leona, a young singer with a dazzling voice that had jetted her to national stardom. Now, just twenty-four hours after her astonishing concert, she was being questioned by Winston, a detective, about the horrific discovery that morning of Jess' lifeless body beside the neighboring swamp.

He found Leona backstage, looking distraught.

"Your concert last night," Winston spoke patiently. "The venue was right next to the swamp, am I correct?”

Leona, with her tear-stained mascara, nodded. "Yes, detective. It was."

"And you had Jess present? Jess with the VIP pass?"

"Yes," Leona replied, her usually confident voice reduced to a mere whisper. "She even met my sister after the show."

"Interesting," Winston muttered, trying to keep his tone neutral. "Because I had a report that she was seen arguing with your sister. She seemed rather threatened."

Leona's face was a mask of sadness as she recalled the event. "My sister? Threatened? I...I saw it happen, she looked scared during their confrontation. Later, Jess also sent a threatening message to my sister after that confrontation. It really upset her and she's been⟦ in⟧ a distressed state since then."

Noticing the grim determination on Leona's face as her thoughts drifted to her sister, Winston probed further. "I heard you're protective of her," he added, watching Leona's reaction.

Visibly shaken, Leona admitted, "I always have been." She dabbed at her eyes with a tissue. "We only have each other. That's why I didn't object when she wanted to come to my martial arts classes."

"Ah, your martial arts classes," Winston interjected. "I have on my record here that you've been seen attending those regularly over the past months."

Leona looked surprised. "Yes, detective. I needed a way to vent out my stress, and I found martial arts comforting."

"Martial arts, hmm?" Winston mused aloud. "Your instructor even mentioned that you've been progressing quite well and he admires your skill with certain weapons. Have you ever handled a sai?"

Fear was written clear on Leona's face as she quietly nodded, understanding where this conversation might be leading to. "Yes, I have. I just purchased a set and have been training with them. They stay in the dojo, though. I swear.”

Little did Leona know, but her confession perfectly fit the narrative Winston was trying to weave. He gave nothing away with his stoic expression.

"I heard," he continued slowly, "that after the concert, Jess was seen headed towards the swamp."

She nodded her head, "Yeah, people sometimes take that route to avoid the traffic..."

The conversation ended, and Winston didn’t probe further. As far as Detective Winston was concerned, he had all the information he needed. In the quiet crevices of a local library, Stephen's life came to an abrupt end, impaled by a trident; now, it's up to the tenacious Detective Winston to unravel the mystery and discern if Sophie or Lowell are responsible.

After another tiring day of working the case, Winston parked his car in a quiet, dimly lit street outside of a popular local gym. Inside was Sophie, his latest person of interest, who had gained notoriety for expressing racist viewpoints at several social gatherings. Witnesses and victims had come forth, stating that Sophie, in her fury, had confronted and threatened individuals belonging to the groups she so openly expressed prejudice against.

Sophie, who was known for her athletic prowess as a professional trident thrower, was amid an intense workout when Winston entered the facility. She was preparing for an upcoming competition, her muscles rippling under the strain of each precise throw. Her unlimited access to the gym's professional equipment made this process much easier.

Winston approached her once she finished her practice throws. "Ms. Sophie," he greeted, his gaze unwavering.

She turned, her eyes blazing with a competitive energy. "Detective Winston," she replied. "Can I help you?"

"Maybe. I'm asking around about a gym guest, Stephen. He was part of your clientele, wasn't he?" He knew the answer, having found that Stephen visited this gym regularly.

Sophie's expression hardened. "Yes," she confirmed. "So what?"

"Stephen has been murdered in the library downtown." Winston noticed Sophie's eyes flicker with surprise, or guilt perhaps. Sophie knew Stephen's routine well. His unusual, long hours spent at the library coincided with the time of the crime, a detail Sophie was well aware of. 

Sophie looked genuinely shocked. "Library?" she echoed, her brows furrowing.

"Yes, the library. Quite an unusual scene, isn't it? Especially when we found a trident near his body. It happens to be identical to the kind here in your gym," Winston added.

Immediately, Sophie blanched. She swiveled her head towards the impressive array of trident equipment, nervously mimicking a laugh. “A trident?” she repeated, “Yes… we do have tridents here for… for our clients.”

Winston changed his line of questioning. "Stephen belonged to a particular minority group, didn't he? One I've heard which you've openly threatened and discriminated against at several social events. Isn't that so?"

Sophie, visibly taken aback, struggled to reply, "I...I have...expressed my views at some social gatherings," she stammered out, her face reddening. "But what's that got to do with Stephen?"

"Well, knowing when Stephen would be at the library," Winston began, "and considering your skill with tridents, the weapon implicated in the crime – I just thought it could be worth looking into."

With those parting words, Winston left the bewildered Sophie in silence inside the gym. This first encounter provided him with more than enough to investigate Sophie further.

Winston found himself at the local train station, a place he often found solace in the comings and goings of people from all walks of life. It was here he knew he would locate Lowell, his next interviewee in regards to Stephen's untimely demise.

Lowell had been the delivery driver for the library's regular book shipments for some time now, making the morning deliveries under the cloaking silence of the pre-dawn air. As Winston deployed his questions, Lowell casually mentioned that his route included the town where the library was. Winston noted the tired dullness in Lowell's eyes as he mentioned his raise from the delivery company - it seemed like the numbing monotony of the job had not changed, nor had Lowell's general lack of enthusiasm about it.

The topic of the recent train accident came up, and what Winston found peculiar was Lowell's nonchalant response to it. Despite the usual shock and upset that strikes most people after such incidents, Lowell appeared almost unfazed, as if it were just another everyday occurrence clashing against his jaded facade.

Winston followed up on an evening invitation for a soiree at Lowell's house. This wasn't his usual cup of tea, but he knew it was an opportunity to further explore Lowell'⟦s⟧ world. The conductor's soirées were known for their unique purpose - showcasing his collection of antiquities, curiosities of historical relevance, and one particular item that never failed to impress.

The antiquated weapon was a focal point of fascination among his guests, a point of conversation that led to their visible amazement.

In the wake of a gruesome flamethrower murder at a local soccer field, seasoned detective Winston steps up to investigate, with suspects Sophia and Larry under his watchful eye.


"Detective Winston," Sophia greeted as she shuffled her cardboard coffee cup in her hands nervously. They were standing on the edge of the football field where the murder had taken place.

"Sophia," Winston nodded, looking out at the half-time huddle of sweaty, tired players - the same scene where Savannah had taken her last breath. 

Sophia was a journalist. She'd been covering the match when Savannah was killed, following her usual line of reportage. Today, she'd been on the field, right where it all happened. Savannah's murder had occurred right at halftime and yet, nobody seemed to know anything. 

"So, it's been a while since your reports on the military exhibition, correct?" Winston asked, keeping his face calm but watchful to catch any change in her expression.

"Yeah,  it was a couple of months ago. I still have the flamethrower I'd managed to keep, for research and, you know... reminders," Sophia said, her gaze flickering toward the field. 

Winston nodded. He knew that keeping memorabilia wasn't uncommon in her trade. Did it provide Sophia with a flamethrower when she needed one?

"Savannah, were you two friends?" Winston asked, keeping an eye on the middle of the field where everything had happened.

"We knew each other... She threatened to reveal my source, ruin my credibility," Sophia sighed, staring at her untouched coffee. 

Sophia's job was at stake, Winston knew; in a field like journalism, credibility mattered.

"Why didn't you tell anyone about the threat?" 

Sophia shifted uncomfortably, "I had heavily invested time and energy in this article. I was protecting my...trust in the field. My source was my lifeline." 

Winston didn't reply but noted her skittishness in revealing her source even now.

"Look, the match is starting!" Sophia pointed out to the field as the whistle blew.

Winston just nodded, eyeing the field where the murder had taken place. If he was to solve this case, he had to sift through the evidence slowly and carefully. Even when it came from a journalist faced with the threat of losing her job and credibility. Even when it was wrapped up in the middle of a football game.

Winston crunched on a stale coffee flavoured donut while wiping away the grim remnants from the computer monitor in his rundown office. He had been staring at the sport section of the local newspaper that spoke about the location of the unfortunate demise of Savannah, a keen enthusiast and promoter of sports in the city, especially soccer who also happened to be a strong opponent of Larry in politics. 

The photograph of the soccer field was chilling, almost like a badly done modern graffiti that had charcoalled the grass in obscene patterns. A flamethrower had been the murder weapon and such a trait of weaponry could point to only a certain group of people who had the experience to⟦ operate⟧ such a complicated tool of destruction, typically war veterans, like Larry.

Larry lived in a secluded house surrounded by woods, and held his position as head of a local survivalist group. Very often, his colleagues complained of Larry turning off his phone and avoiding them after work. This lack of response to text messages, calls, or any other means of digital communication could only be explained by Larry's choice to retreat in solidarity and bare minimal social contact. 

Winston sighed, pushed away the paper, and prepared to visit Larry. As usual, in unsociable fashion, Larry declined Winston's invitation to join his colleagues. 

Winston knocked on the rustic door of Larry's eerie looking cabin. When Larry opened the door, he looked like he had just finished a drill. He was sweating, hair a disheveled mess, his posture was rigid and alert. His eyes darted to his wristwatch, hinting towards a habit that he exhibited during various events, checking time frequently. "Larry," Winston said.

Larry recognised him and invited him in albeit reluctantly. A quick glance around the room was enough to see survivalist instincts visible in every corner. In amongst the survival gear was a flamethrower, a common item found in survivalists tool kits. But Winston ignored it and tried to talk politics. 

Larry seemed keen to steer the conversation towards Savannah - his fiery political rival. Winston learned Larry had a habit of attending all the political rallies personally. Savannah's recent rally was public, held downtown at the center square, and as always, Larry had been present. 

Trying to make Larry more comfortable, Winston asked Larry about his social life and why he declined invitations to join others. Larry just shrugged, avoided Winston's gaze, and said he wasn't interested in what others were doing.

His answers lacked conviction, but Winston held his professionalism and didn't push any further. He thanked Larry for his time and left.<turn|>

In the wake of Lola's mysterious katana-driven demise at a secluded mountain cabin, Detective Winston finds himself entangled in a web of suspicion, with Isabelle and Frank peering anxiously from its corners.

Winston gazed contemplatively at a mountain cabin photo where Lola had met her end. He grimaced as his gaze landed on the katana. This was not a run-of-the-mill crime; it was seemingly conducted with a professional touch.

Bringing himself back from the troubling images, he turned his attention to Isabelle. As Lola's life coach, she could potentially shed some light on the complexities surrounding her death. 

Flicking novel-like through an accumulation of notes, he discovered that Isabelle was not as open as most coaches. She engaged with her clients predominantly through privacy-focused platforms and kept any personal details off public forums. The agreement she held with her clients also contained a clause about prioritizing privacy and confiding in her seemed to be one of her requirements, and David --the other man Lola had an affair with-- was no exception. He confided in her, quite frequently as it turned out.

However, what caught his attention was a note hinting at her discovery of intimate text messages between Lola and another man. That's why she confided uneasily with David more, ushering them into lengthy personal conversations and extraneous time spent alone. They had far more interactions outside the coaching sessions than was typical.

Pulling into Isabelle's driveway, Winston noticed the peace that surrounded her home. Inside, Isabelle waited patiently on an austere chair, a sharp contrast to the decor of the rest of the home.

"Busy day?" A plain, professional question to start off with. 

"Indeed. Three sessions at the Dojo and then some client interactions," Isabelle replied. 

"Wow, that's a tight routine. At the Dojo, I assume you work with the Katana?" Winston tried to keep his tone casual.

"That's correct. I try to keep them in the best condition... sharpening included."

Her house was decidedly sparse, but one room was markedly different. A room dedicated to her treasured collection of Katana. Delicate, sharp, deadly works of art.

Isabelle was not one to engage unnecessarily; she had expressed as much. But there was one occasion where she did seem to talk, quite a bit actually. To David.

"Have you met David outside of the coaching sessions?" Winston asked, as he examined one of the Katanas. 

"Yes, a few times. Our schedules happen to coincide," she responded, her eyes averted.

"And some of these encounters were in regards to the intimate messages Lola was sharing with the other man?"

"Yes, that's correct."

"In connection with Lola, perhaps?"

Isabelle's gaze hardened. "Lola was stepping over boundaries - I saw her kissing David."

The session ended with more questions than answers for Winston. He casually bid her goodbye, having established she preferred minimal social interactions.

"Gotta head back, Isabelle, can't keep the precinct waiting. You have a good day now." He put on his hat and walked out, leaving Isabelle with her thoughts.

Detective Winston sat hunched over his quaint oak desk, his dark eyes scanning⟦ over⟧ the phone records of the deceased, Lola. He jotted down a quick note - Lola had dialed one number numerous times, the number belonging to a certain Frank. It seemed Lola made a habit of contacting him.

His notes also mentioned that multiple witnesses had recently spotted Frank practicing with his Katanas at a local martial arts studio. His swordsmanship had certainly improved, it showed dedication.

The following day, Winston found himself driving up the mountain to meet with Frank, a well-respected biologist having an impressive and crucially vital academic career. Frank's workspace was littered with numerous awards and commendations highlighting the value of his work; it was clear that his reputation was important to him.

"Good afternoon, Frank," Detective Winston greeted, extending a hand.

Frank looked up from his microscope and shook the detective's hand, "Afternoon, detective. What brings you here?"

"Lola invited you to her cabin under the semblance of a work retreat, isn't it?" Winston asked, leaning against the lab desk.

"Yes," Frank replied reluctantly, "But I never told anyone else about that."

Winston nodded and changed the topic, grabbing one of the photos off the table. It was shot a few days ago, Lola and Frank seemed to be in a heated discussion, "Care to share what this altercation was about?"

"Nothing serious, just some professional disagreements," Frank dismissed hurriedly, seeming eager to move past the topic.

As Winston glanced around the room, he noticed something else; A pair of katanas meticulously maintained and displayed on the wall. "You have an interest in martial arts, Frank?"

Frank seemed to relax a little, leaning back from the microscope, "Yes, I've been taking classes recently. It helps me focus."

"And what about these?" Winston asked, indicating towards the Katanas.

"Ah those..." Frank trailed off. "Well yes, I've been practicing with them, they're my favorite weapon of choice in martial arts," he admitted, quickly adding, "but they're only for practice."

Winston headed to the local hardware store after the meeting to confirm another fact. Frank had indeed bought a sharpening stone just a couple of days ago.

At the end of the day, he checked out Frank's public schedule - it was free on the day Lola got murdered, just as his hunch had indicated. He cross-checked with some bystanders, who also confirmed seeing Frank near the mountain cabin on the same day.

As Winston wrapped up his day of investigation, he couldn't help but remember the one last crucial piece of information. Lola had been blackmailing Frank with evidence of academic misconduct, tarnishing the career he was so proud of.<turn|>

When fitness enthusiast Uma is ominously murdered with a vial of acid at her local gym, it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery between the two prime suspects, Irving and Addison.

Detective Winston was indoors on another stifling California afternoon. His attention was fixed on the Irving case, a case that kept him on his toes for several days now. A screenwriter suspected in the murder of a fellow gym goer. He couldn’t help but feel the increasing pressure of the time crunch.

Irving was not an ordinary man. Winston had discovered from the interviews and police records that the guy particularly had some weird habits. Irving, it seemed, was battling insomnia and was unable to sleep in his own home at night. During these restless nights, he would busy himself with his notebooks. Often, he was seen at the fitness center, sketching intriguing symbols into his notebook, which he always carried along with his pencil. He would leave home with these immediately after sunset.

One specific detail that struck the detective was Irving's fascination with themes and symbols of the past, particularly those formed by ancient gravestones. These ancient symbols were found in notations and sketches strewn across his notebooks. It was curious to Winston how an old world art found a home in the hands of a modern screenwriter.

His insomniac late-night habits weren't the only thing that raised suspicions, though. Irving also was a member at the same fitness center Uma frequented, spotted regularly training late into the night. The very same fitness center that was the scene of the crime. The records substantiated his presence late on the night of the murder. Like the deceased Uma, he seemed to utilized the solitude that the near-empty gym provided, allowing him ample time alone.

The lines on Winston's forehead became more pronounced as he read on. He found a strange connection between both Uma's and Irving's lives. Not only did they work out at the same gym, but they also shared a professional conflict. Reports indicated that Uma had discovered Irving's success was largely built on her own work which he'd plagiarized. Fearing public humiliation and the definite demise of his screenwriting career, Irving had a lot to lose. To make matters worse for Irving, Uma, the aggrieved, had threatened to expose his deceit to the public.

The tension of the case was truly weighing on Winston. He sighed, leaning back from his desk. Questions in his mind demanded answers that weren't there yet. So, he decided to continue with the investigation, waiting for the breakthrough that would add some clarity to the clouded picture. He had a late-night meeting with the prime suspect, Irving, in the pipeline. It was indeed time to probe further and extract some answers from the silence of the night.

Detective Winston admired the modern glow of the fitness center that served as his next stop in the investigation. The thudding of footfalls on running machines, the humming of weight machines, and the faint scent of sweat and disinfectant whispered of a place that had teetered on the edge of life and death.

"Lookin' to join?" came a voice from behind him. He languidly turned to find Addison, the local trainer.

"No. Detective Winston, on official police business," he presented his badge.

The sour taste of surprise was evident on Addison's face, "We're an excellent gym with a friendly vibe; it's a shame. You don't say, a detective?"

"I've checked the fitness center security cameras," Winston watched as Addison pressed his lips together, "Noticed you were entering the gym shortly before time of Uma's death."

Addison placed a hand on a weight machine, lowering his gaze to his feet. "Uma? You mean my client, Uma? We were scheduled for a training session that day."

Winston opened his notebook, scanning his notes, "You have a background in chemistry, is that right?"

Addison looked up from his shoes, "Yeah, I even teach it at the high school. Possess a chemistry degree and recently purchased a chemistry set for demonstration."

"Interesting. The set contains vials of acid, science class protocol?" Winston asked, his brow furrowing.

"Absolutely, controlled experiments to teach risk and safety," Addison said, transported into the world of academia. The detective noticed a flicker in Addison’s expression as he continued to speak but brushed it off, it meant nothing yet.

A few people from the gym had crowded around now. They watched as Winston asked, "Can you recall Uma saying anything about the honesty of the staff or maybe about any missing equipment?"

"Well," Addison began, rubbing his neck, "Uma did once vouch for me, said I was honest and commendable, a good character, you know." He looked around the room and swallowed. "And yes, she did mention once about missing equipment. Unfortunately, she also stumbled upon some CCTV footage of me taking some expensive equipment. I had intended to return it, it was a mistake. "

As Winston watched the gym members disperse, he looked back at Addison. "So, Uma caught you stealing from the fitness center. That must've been uncomfortable for you. It surfaced in the investigation that fitness equipment has been reported missing recently. Uma seemed to have discovered the theft."

Addison suddenly seemed to find the floor tiles fascinating. "Uma was a good woman," he said quietly. "It's a shame what happened to her."

"Agreed," Winston replied, closing his notebook. "Keep a clear schedule, Addison. We'll be in touch."

As Winston exited the gym he took one more glance at Addison through the large glass panes. Cold air nipped at his face and Winston pondered the car ride back to the station.<turn|>

Cold sweat trickled down Winston’s spine as he perused the grim photos of the crime scene at the mosque. Winston fished the statement reports from his pile of case files, which stated that Kent and Julia were last seen together at the mosque.  Kent had been poisoned with snake venom, a tricky murder weapon to trace. His victim, Kent, was Julia's cousin and had last been seen at the mosque with her before he met his unfortunate fate.

His next stop was clear. He pulled his coat close against the biting wind and snow. Silicon Valley, estate of one Julia. Inside, he found Julia embroiled in what seemed an exhaustive pile of legal documents. From their exchange, he learned that she was currently tangled up in a knotty lawsuit, where the opposing party had a good deal to gain, financially that is.

Stepping into what he could only describe as a mini laboratory, a brave new world peered back at him. Labeled samples cluttered the table, one of which was a snake venom sample. Julia was trained as a herpetologist and her job involved working with venomous snakes, she explained this to Winston while also showing him her work with venomous snakes.

As they moved⟦ past⟧ countless terrariums, Winston paused in front of a portrait on the mantel. “That’s Kent,” Julia sighed. “Always the favored one, especially by Grandpa. In his latest will, everything was left to him. The will was initially expected to be in my favor, but, he bypassed me completely," Julia said. Her voice turned bitter as she revealed these shocking discoveries about her cousin, Kent.

Changing the topic to something less contentious, she mentioned that both of them used to frequent the same mosque for prayers, the very place where Kent was last seen alive by people, before she added, "And we were together at the mosque that same day." Her tone hardened as she described an altercation with Kent she had had earlier that day at the mosque. The tension was palpable as she revealed her own cousin had been secretly helping the opposition in the ongoing legal battle.

Winston nodded, took a few final notes, and bid his farewell, a gust of wind blowing in with the opening of the front door. His footsteps crunched the snow beneath his boots and the stark contrast of his solitary car in the vast white providence painted an odd yet mystic picture. As he drove off, the silhouette of Julia’s house receded, but the flicker of suspicion stayed kindled in his mind.

Winston sauntered into the buzzing fairgrounds. His worn Panama hat tilted, casting a shadow over his contoured face as he surveyed the spectacle of the annual town fair. Ronald, the man he had come to see, was easy to spot - standing tall in his uniform as security for the event.

"Ronald?" Winston called out after weaving through the crowd of cotton-candy eaters and parched parents.

A sharp look from Ronald confirmed his identity.

Ever the expert at concealing his hand, Winston lightly grazed the topic. "I hear you’re pretty experienced with snakes. Handle 'em at the zoo, right? A zoo with quite a variety of venomous snakes, so I've heard."

A flicker of pride sparked in Ronald's eyes. "Yes, that's right. From rattlers to mambas, we have them all. I have the keys to all animal enclosures, even the Venomous Serpent Exhibit."

"Must be quite a job, wrangling all those snakes," said Winston. "Especially with the variety of venomous species you have. They can be lethal with their venom."

"You bet. But it's all about understanding and respect," Ronald’s eyes reflected the love for his job.

That’s when Winston changed tactics. He didn't have the luxury of time; the fair was busy, and he sensed Ronald wouldn't stay guard at his post for long. 

"I need to talk about some documents," he said. Before he even finished his sentence, the color drained from Ronald’s face. "Documents linking you to past misdemeanors. They were found on a man named Kent."

The denial came swift and in violence. "This is preposterous! That man was maligning me; I did nothing wrong!”

A shrill kiddy ride whirled inches from them, momentarily deafening Winston to anything else Ronald had to say. By the time the wooden cars clattered to a stop, Ronald was sprinting the other way. 

He was no longer at his post, no longer within sight, and no longer within Winston’s reach for further questions. For now. The detective adjusted his hat, scanning the field. Winston knew he had started unraveling traces, but he’d need to tread carefully here on out. Ronald was spooked, and even the deadliest snake wouldn't strike unless cornered.<turn|>

Winston nodded, "Yes, she said she will be available."

John, a night-worker, usually checked his surroundings before heading to bed. From his window, one had a clear view of Lucy's house. Winston made a mental note of it before he walked towards her porch light's glow.

Inside, Lucy cleared her throat, "I'm usually in bed by nine, but you're welcome to stay. Would you like something to drink, detective?" 

"No, thank you," He responded, letting his gaze move over the room.

"I had to pick up some of Dwayne's things", Anthony said, hand unconsciously stroking the keychain. "His woman couldn’t do it, she's a wreck."

"You had keys to his car?" Winston prompted.

"Well, yes, we were friends after all," Anthony replied, confirming his synaptic tie to Dwayne's automobile.

"To convince him about your beliefs?" Winston posed, a touch of humanity in his tone.

"No, to make him understand my art!" Anthony's voice was emphatic. But he didn’t admit to painting with gold.

"There were disagreements then?" Winston asked, almost rhetorically.

A deep sigh rasped out from Anthony's mouth. "Yes, often. Unfortunately, I was unable to win him over."

He looked down at his hands, the same hands that relentlessly splashed beautiful, and often disturbing, illusions onto canvas. And then a grim realization reflected on his face, a bitter parting comment reminding him of the deep offense Dwayne’s criticism might have caused. In a chilling turn of events, Rose is found lifeless in a car, killed by a vial of acid, leading Detective Winston to the affluent suspects, Daisy and Dexter.

Winston pulled into the parking lot of an electronics store, neat rows of televisions shining through the large storefront window. He fought a sigh as he approached the doors, remembering the usual jumble of gizmos and gadgets that never failed to make him feel outdated. 

Inside, a friendly-looking man with round glasses and a slightly off-kilter smile stood behind a counter, engaged in a quiet conversation with a customer. Seeing Winston, he excused himself and approached with a warm greeting.

"Officer, how can I help you today?" 

"I'm Detective Winston. I hear you've got a batch of new batteries in stock?"

Dexter's smile faltered a bit, "Yes, sir. Came in last week. Anything specific you're looking for?" After an uncertain pause, he added, "Our stock varies from these small pencil batteries to some real heavy ones, you see."

Winston gave a noncommittal answer, observing Dexter surreptitiously. The man had a certain peculiar charm; he seemed more like an impish professor than a sales associate at an electronics store. Following the conversation, Winston found his gaze drawn to a large cardboard box residing in one corner of the store. However, noting the interest, Dexter mentioned his personal collection at home.

"Ah, customers just love looking through that large box of trinkets over there.", he gently scratched his chin and a soft smile played on his lips, "And there's another similar treasure chest in my living room at my place too." Catching his nostalgic glance, it dawned on Winston that Dexter always included items into a similar box in his living room at his home following each customer visit to the store.

By the time Winston decided to leave the store, he felt sure of his next course of action. He headed over to Dexter's home. The house was, truth be told, quite modest but left a comforting impression. The first thing he noticed was a bookshelf overflowing with chemistry textbooks, not the staple for sales associates, he thought ironically, recognizing a few from his own school days.

He found himself staring at a cluttered table which held a photo album. Picking it up, he flipped through. Each photo had a caption underneath, reminiscing good times spent with the individuals pictured. As he took in this personal element, he recalled a town gathering where the lighthearted Rose, having discovered an embarrassing picture of Dexter, couldn't stop laughing directly at him and sharing it with everyone attending the gathering. The picture was now a town legend, circulating far and wide.

As he put the album down, Winston glanced towards the wall clock. The late afternoon sun was shifting into evening. He decided to wrap up the visit. On his way⟦ out⟧, Dexter engaged him in some small talk about their shared love for the town's food. It was during their conversation that Winston discovered Dexter had previously studied chemistry in college, majoring in industrial acids. Winston thanked him politely and went on his way.

The detective, Winston, had strong coffee in his hand as he reviewed the case files laid out in front of him. His current assignment was the murder of Rose, who was found dead in her car by means of an acid attack. The type of acid was identical to those found in Daisy's performances. The perpetrator got away, leaving only a vial as evidence.

Rose had frequent parking spots, and her car was often seen in the lot near the locals' favorite music venue. Upon inquiry, Daisy shared how she often incorporated the acids into her performances for dramatic effects. Witnesses from the concert reported seeing Daisy and Rose leaving the venue together after the show. They appeared to be the only ones in the car. Daisy didn't hesitate to confirm, "Oh, yes, Rose and I left the venue together. She was kind enough to offer me a lift, as my own ride bailed out."

As Winston left the venue, his phone buzzed, reminding him of Daisy's recent addition to Rose's sizable life insurance policy just a month ago. Winston's eyebrow lifted slightly. This matches the eyewitness reports placing Glenn at the zoo that day, and another reporting a bulky blue bag on his person.

"A tool bag to the zoo, Glenn?" Winston raised the question.

Glenn’s smile started to fade, "I usually carry it around with me for work, it's got all my tools." He said, a flicker of unease in his eyes, "In case I need them, you know."

Winston found these elements forming a clear image, but he knew better than to impress suspicion where it wasn't explicitly warranted. He would need more. More conversations, more observations, and more unearthing of Glenn’s peculiar behaviours.

Detective Winston brushed crumbs of his sandwich onto his pile of case files. His latest, involving a man named Walter, was proving rather intriguing. Walter had been involved in some questionable business deals... to put it mildly. An interesting detail in all this was that Walter's murder had occurred during an excursion to the local zoo.

Winston squinted his eyes at the witness statement in front of him, given by the key character in this tragedy, a man named Dennis. Dennis had been living with Walter as a foster son and had been a reluctant observer to Walter's illegal doings. He'd had a fear of Walter that was believable in its intensity. His words stuttered and shook on the page as he described how Walter threatened him with dire consequences.

Winston grabbed his keys and headed out to meet with Dennis at his worksite, the lad worked construction, a fact confirmed by Winston's preliminary check.

Approaching the site, Winston saw Dennis working with a nail gun, a tool that looked like a second skin on the young man's hand. Winston could see the professional ease of Dennis wielding the heavy tool and hit his targets with precision.

"Good afternoon, Dennis," Winston greeted him. The young man paused and turned towards him, his face a flicker of honest surprise. "Oh, hi, detective", he replied.

"Dennis", Winston started, "Can you confirm that Walter had invited you to the zoo that day?"

A chill ran over Dennis's face as he replied, "Yes, that's correct."

"Do you often go to the zoo?"

The young man got a far-off look in his eyes, "Yeah, we used to go often. Bonding.. they call it.."

"I see," Winston responded," and about your purchase at the hardware store the day before the visit..."

Dennis looked confused, "Yes, I frequently buy supplies for work. That day, it was a box of nails for my nail gun."

Looking around the site party in admiration and part nostalgia, Winston asked, "Work keeps you busy?"

Grinning at that, Dennis said, "It does, detective, but I had a free day... the day Walter died." His voice caught on the last sentence.

"Alright Dennis, thank you for your time", Winston said, turning on his heel to leave.

The zoo itself was Winston's next stop. He noted it was unusually quiet and several areas were deserted. Perfect chance for a murder, he mused, not that Dennis did it. There's plenty yet to uncover.

As he was exiting, Winston's phone buzzed. His latest query results for Dennis had arrived. The lad did visit a hardware store the day before Walter's murder. And the purchase details matched Dennis's account of buying nails for his nail gun.

Winston buckled up in his car and sighed heavily. There was a sense of fear creeping up his spine, not his own but one that belonged to a young construction worker. A troubled foster son. A possible suspect. A probable witness.<turn|>
